stem: An index number formula satisfies the time-reversal test if, when the base year and the current year are interchanged, the product of the two indices equals 1. Which of the following indices satisfies this test?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Laspeyres uses fixed base-year weights; when base and current are swapped the product of the two Laspeyres indices does not equal 1 in general.
Paasche uses current-year weights; swapping base and current gives the same asymmetry problem, so the time-reversal test fails for Paasche too.
Neither Laspeyres nor Paasche satisfies the time-reversal test individually because each relies on a single year's quantities as fixed weights.

Fisher Ideal Index = sqrt(L * P). When base and current are swapped, each factor inverts and the product of the forward and backward Fisher indices equals exactly 1, satisfying the time-reversal test.

explanation: The time-reversal test requires: I(0,1) * I(1,0) = 1. Laspeyres and Paasche each fail because their weights are tied to one specific year, creating asymmetry. Fisher, as the geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche, satisfies both the time-reversal test and the factor-reversal test, making it the only one of these three that passes both adequacy tests.

explanation_sections.punchline: Only Fisher satisfies the time-reversal test; Laspeyres and Paasche each fail because their weights anchor to one year.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the property: time-reversal test = I(0->1) * I(1->0) = 1. Check each index: Laspeyres keeps q0 fixed (fails when years swap); Paasche keeps q1 fixed (same problem). Fisher averages both so it cancels the asymmetry.
explanation_sections.lesson: Fisher is called ideal precisely because it passes both tests (time-reversal and factor-reversal). Laspeyres and Paasche each pass only factor-reversal after adjustment. Memorise: Fisher = both tests satisfied.
explanation_sections.timing: About 30-45 seconds. Pure recall. The trap is thinking both Laspeyres and Paasche pass the time-reversal test.
